questions.title: What does AI need beyond tokens and components?
questions.description: Tokens give values. Component properties give options. Neither explains when to use something or why an exception exists. That lives in documentation and component contracts: expected behavior, allowed combinations, accessibility requirements. The more explicit those are, the better the agent gets. Then the real question is whether it actually applies them.

questions.title: How much guidance is enough?
questions.description: Less than you’d think. One big AGENTS.md is tempting, but agents struggle with vague prose and files that never end. What seems to work better: a short file that points to where everything else lives, so the agent doesn’t read the whole system every run, and rules that grow each time the agent gets something wrong. For the rules that really matter, lint rules. Agents can’t skip those.

questions.title: Where do busy teams start?
questions.description: Teams are getting smaller, and “make the design system AI-ready” is one more big task on an already full list. I’d start small: a quick health check, then one problem that keeps coming back. An undocumented decision, a misleading example, a component people struggle with. One fix. One check. Then the next.
questions.linkLabel: Don’t make your design system AI-ready yet

questions.title: What comes after “AI-ready”?
questions.description:
Some teams already let agents maintain parts of their design system. Once a system is in good shape (audited, gaps fixed, agents know where to look), it can start taking care of itself. A component changes, an agent spots what no longer matches, fixes it, and opens a pull request. Audits and health checks could run the same way.

Agents do the work. We define what’s “right,” and test for it. That’s the idea behind an agentic design system, and what I’m exploring now.

about: Hey, I’m Érica. I’ve been in design for 15+ years and somewhere along the way became the person who gets excited about taking messy, complex things and making them work.
For a long time, that’s meant design systems, where I found my passion.

Now that AI is in the picture, there’s a whole new set of questions to work through. I’m exploring them here and writing about the wins, the awkward moments, and the “well, that didn’t work” parts at Design Systems Unfiltered.

whoami.body:
Hey, I’m Érica. Brazilian, based in Germany, remote-first, with 15+ years in design.

Most of that time has gone into design systems: component audits, Figma libraries, tokens, documentation, and helping teams through migrations. Now I’m exploring what changes when AI starts using them too.

- Getting a design system back in sync: an audit of 62 components across Figma, React, and Flutter, then the library changes and migration guidance that followed.
- Maturing a design system beyond components: a look back at a year of library changes, pattern documentation, support tracking, and day-to-day work with product designers.

systems.body:
Components and tokens are part of it. So are the rules for using them, the differences between implementations, and the steps for moving to a new version.

One example: Disabled and Loading were values of a Figma State property, while the coded component treated them as separate booleans. So the Figma component changed to match.
